title: Footnotes without losing place
summary: Inspect a note and return to the exact reading anchor.
problem: Opening a note can displace the passage, cover it or return the reader to the top of a chapter.
solution: Attach the note to its text anchor and preserve its parts: origin reference, quoted phrase, explanatory text and alternative reading where supplied. Choose inline expansion, a mobile sheet or a study panel by note length and available space.
failure: Hover-only access; a modal with no usable close control; merging quoted wording and editorial explanation; closing to a different reading position.
test: Test opening and closing with touch, keyboard and screen reader at large text sizes. Confirm focus and the visible reading position return to the note anchor.

variants.when: Mobile space is limited and the note is longer
variants.tradeoff: A sheet can cover the verse and needs focus return

variants.when: Sustained study benefits from seeing both surfaces
variants.tradeoff: A panel costs reading width and needs a visible anchor

faith: Do not label translation footnotes as AI commentary. Publisher material and personal notes have different ownership and permissions.
takeaway: Attach the note to its text anchor and preserve its parts: origin reference, quoted phrase, explanatory text and alternative reading where supplied.

editorial_review.purpose: A reader wants an edition note without losing the passage.
editorial_review.benefit: A local preview can answer a small question without a separate reading journey.
editorial_review.drawback: Inline expansion moves text; a sheet can obscure the verse; a panel needs room.
editorial_review.differences: Quick checking benefits from a preview. Extended study may need both text and note visible. Large text and keyboard focus affect the best surface.
editorial_review.question: Can the reader identify whose note this is and return to its anchor?
editorial_review.check: Open a long note at large text size, follow a reference and return. Check scroll and keyboard focus.

title: Editorial distinctions survive reflow
summary: Preserve poetry, headings and translation additions without forcing a rigid layout.
problem: Small screens and enlarged text can flatten meaningful structure or turn editorial headings into apparent verse content.
solution: Reflow paragraphs and preserve relative poetic structure. Distinguish section headings from Scripture. Explain translator-supplied words when the edition marks them. Verse navigation can coexist with continuous prose.
failure: Shrinking text to preserve a desktop layout; treating each verse as an unrelated box; calling translation additions AI-generated text.
test: Test narrow screens, enlarged fonts and spoken output. Can readers recognise a heading, poetic grouping and a translation addition without relying only on colour?

variants.tradeoff: Explain the convention without cluttering every word

variants.caption: Indentation follows meaning at larger text sizes.
items: poem|First poetic line /  Second related line / Next poetic line
variants.when: Line grouping contributes to poetic meaning
variants.tradeoff: Indentation must survive narrow widths

variants.caption: Headings and verse labels support, rather than fragment, reading.

variants.tradeoff: Verse labels must remain discoverable

faith: Preserve the chosen edition’s conventions. A structure standard informs meaning; it does not prescribe one screen component.
takeaway: Reflow paragraphs and preserve relative poetic structure.

editorial_review.purpose: A reader encounters poetry, headings or words marked as supplied by translators.
editorial_review.benefit: Preserving meaningful distinctions helps readers understand the edition’s editorial choices.
editorial_review.drawback: Too many visual conventions can distract; too few can erase meaningful distinctions.
editorial_review.differences: Someone new to the edition may need a short explanation. Experienced readers may prefer less repeated help. Narrow screens still need meaningful indentation.
editorial_review.question: Is this distinction from the source, the publisher or our interface?
editorial_review.check: Review poetry, headings and translation additions at large text sizes. Ask readers to explain the distinction without guessing.

title: Original media before synthesis
summary: Let readers inspect the source behind an explanation.
problem: A video excerpt or AI summary can sound convincing while hiding who said it and where the statement occurs.
solution: Use media cards with creator, original source, duration and relevant time range. Link supported claims to precise excerpts. Offer transcript and original context; playback starts deliberately and failure leaves the conversation readable.
failure: Autoplay; incorrect time windows; edited clips that reverse meaning; source opinions presented as consensus; a missing video hidden behind a confident synthesis.
test: Check whether every evidence claim is supported at the linked position. Test unavailable media, captions, returning from playback and the context before and after an excerpt.

variants.tradeoff: A link or transcript may be the only permitted alternative

faith: This applies to sermons, teaching videos, podcasts and courses. Association with a verse is not proof of a particular interpretation.
takeaway: Use media cards with creator, original source, duration and relevant time range.

editorial_review.purpose: A reader wants to inspect a sermon, video or audio source.
editorial_review.benefit: Source metadata and a transcript allow inspection beyond a confident summary.
editorial_review.drawback: A short clip may distort its surrounding argument; timestamps can be wrong.
editorial_review.differences: Caption and transcript access matter for people who cannot hear or cannot play media in their current setting.
editorial_review.question: Would the surrounding material change how this excerpt is understood?
editorial_review.check: Check whether every evidence claim is supported at the linked position. Test unavailable media, captions, returning from playback and the context before and after an excerpt.

title: Passage preview opens a full reader
summary: Keep long Scripture readable without flooding the conversation.
problem: A full chapter inside a small chat card can create nested scrolling. Aggressive truncation can hide what the user asked to read.
solution: Choose among an excerpt card opening a full reader, complete inline expansion for manageable passages, and a dedicated reading surface for sustained reading. Name the requested range, edition and visible range. Inline expansion uses the main conversation scroll rather than a nested text scroll; provide Collapse and retain an anchor when collapsing. A full reader can be a sheet on small screens or a side panel on wider screens, with an explicit return to the same conversation place. For cross-chapter ranges, preserve every boundary and continuation. If complete text is requested, provide a clearly labelled route to it rather than silently summarising. If edition rights or availability prevent full display, explain the limit and offer a permitted destination.
failure: Unmarked omissions; two competing scroll regions; a summary presented as the original passage; returning to the top of the chat.
test: Test a short verse, long passage, complete chapter request and large text. Can readers recognise omissions, reach the whole text and return to the same conversation position? Test inline expansion and collapse, cross-chapter ranges, sheet and panel return, multiple passage cards, unavailable editions and the final verse at large text size.

purpose_lens.test: Give someone a multi-verse request, ask them to inspect the entire passage and then return to their question. Verify the first and last requested verses, not just whether a card opened.

title: The player works without the screen
summary: Support listening as a complete mode of use.
problem: An audio Bible may depend on a visual reader for basic navigation and lose usefulness when the device is locked.
solution: Make current passage, playback, interruption and resumption available through suitable device and accessibility controls. Offer speed and sleep options where supported. Preserve the last listening position and a route into reading.
failure: Voice-only stopping; a hidden player; resuming at the wrong chapter; treating listening as microphone consent.
test: Test lock-screen use, interruptions, headphones, connectivity loss and switching to text. Confirm what the selected edition actually supports.

purpose_lens.test: Try playback with the screen off, an interruption and a return to the text. Ask listeners to choose where listening ends. Measure task completion and control without treating listening duration as spiritual benefit.

editorial_review.check: Lock the device, interrupt playback and resume. Confirm the passage and position; repeat offline where downloads are supported.

title: Playback and reading positions can differ
summary: Follow the narration without forcing the reader to follow every movement.
problem: Someone may scroll ahead or revisit an earlier verse while playback continues. Automatic following can repeatedly pull them back.
solution: Show the current playback anchor separately from the viewport. Let users follow or explore freely, then deliberately return to the spoken passage. Use continuous text where the task is sustained reading.
failure: Automatic recentering after manual scroll; stopping playback whenever someone explores; treating the visible paragraph as the actual playback position.
test: Scroll away during playback, change text size and return to the spoken verse. Does each position remain understandable?

title: Choose a devotional format
summary: Compare a continuous reading, a sequence of cards and a chaptered audio session.
problem: A swipe-based story can hide its length or force unwanted audio, prayer or disclosure before allowing progress.
solution: Separate the content model from its presentation: Scripture, reflection, video, prayer and silence retain their identity in each format. A continuous page supports scanning; multi-page steps offer explicit pacing; story-style cards can combine short media segments. Offer visible Previous, Next and an outline rather than relying on swipes. Avoid timed advance for text by default. Audio needs pause, chapter navigation, transcript and an explicit end. Switching formats should preserve a semantic section where correspondence exists; do not invent word-level synchronisation.
failure: A story that advances before the reader finishes; tiny text fitted to one card; essential teaching available only in uncaptioned video; media playback counted as prayer; a disabled Next button until personal disclosure; automatic playback of another devotional.
test: Move through a mixed-media session with sound off, large text, keyboard or screen reader navigation, and an unavailable video. Leave during a section and return. Verify the selected content version and section are restored, and ask what is required versus optional.

title: Progress and streaks
summary: Choose between a saved place, completion and a shared date. Explain what the record means.
problem: A display can help someone find their place while also suggesting how well they are doing spiritually. Opened content, marked completion, calendar position and consistency are different records.
solution: Define each state before designing the indicator. Store the saved passage separately from sessions the person marks complete and the dates assigned by a plan. Allow completion to be corrected. Rescheduling changes dates without filling gaps or erasing notes. Explain whether recorded activity is private or shared before enabling group visibility. Offer a clear next action; do not require a progress dashboard to reach the reading.
failure: Silently counting an opened passage as read; resetting completion when changing dates; presenting calendar delay as spiritual failure; using colour alone for status; turning a private activity record into a group ranking; claiming app activity captures reading elsewhere.
test: Ask readers to find their next session, correct an accidental completion and join today’s group reading without completing earlier sessions. Repeat with a screen reader, large text and an offline update. Ask what the display implies about them and who can see it. Compare usefulness and pressure with a saved-place-only version.

faith: A record can serve a chosen discipline without becoming a verdict on the person. Daily reading may matter deeply to someone; a period of absence tells the app little about their faithfulness. Describe what is known and leave space for the person’s own account of its meaning.
takeaway: Show the information needed for the next decision. A saved place may be enough; add completion for a bounded plan and calendar position when a shared date matters. Keep consistency optional and separate.
flow: Open the plan at a useful next step; identify any shared date separately from the saved place.
Let the reader mark a session complete or undo that mark. Opening the session alone does not silently complete it.
When changing dates, preview the new schedule and explain group effects. Keep completion, notes and saved position intact.
After offline use, show whether the change has synced. Resolve conflicting updates without silently inventing completion.
Let the person finish, hide optional history or pause reminders without losing access to the plan.

purpose_lens.assumption: A number invites comparison. Before adding one, decide whether it helps the reader orient, finish a chosen sequence or coordinate with others. More visible progress is not automatically more useful.
situations: Receive today’s passage
Show the daily offering with an optional archive. Yesterday can remain available without becoming an overdue assignment.
Finish a chosen plan
Show marked completion against a clear endpoint. Let someone correct the record or stop without losing their notes.
Support a chosen habit
If someone wants consistency feedback, define what counts and let them hide it. A streak introduces an incentive beyond orientation; assess its effect on motivation and return after interruption.
purpose_lens.question: What does this display help the reader decide—and what might they believe it says about their spiritual life?
purpose_lens.test: Compare a saved place with added completion or consistency feedback. Ask about control, usefulness and pressure over time, including after missed sessions. Do not infer motivation from the number of opens.
purpose_lens.guide_label: Reading rhythms, daily offerings and progress

editorial_review.purpose: Someone wants to find their next reading, finish a selected sequence or rejoin a group’s current passage.
editorial_review.benefit: A clearly labelled record can reduce uncertainty and help the person make the next choice.
editorial_review.drawback: Visible gaps or counts can become a source of pressure. App records also miss reading, listening or reflection that happens elsewhere.
editorial_review.differences: A self-directed reader may need only a saved place. A plan participant may value completion. A group member may need today’s date and their own position at once. These purposes can change between sessions.
editorial_review.question: Is the display describing an activity, coordinating a date or implying a judgment about the reader?
editorial_review.check: Have readers resume, undo completion and change dates. Ask what the record means, whether it feels useful and who can see it. Test comprehension and pressure separately from retention.

title: A flexible reading rhythm
summary: Help someone choose a reading rhythm—and adjust it when life changes.
problem: A rigid daily plan can become unusable when someone’s schedule, ability or life situation changes.
solution: Let the person choose between a dated plan and a sequence that waits for them. Offer reminders separately. Before pausing or moving dates, explain what will change and preserve completed sessions, notes and the saved place. For a group plan, distinguish a personal adjustment from a change to the shared calendar.
failure: Forced daily goals; erasing progress after rescheduling; presenting missed days as moral failures.
test: Study real reading rhythms, including irregular and shared practice. Can users change pace without losing their place or feeling penalised?

variants.tradeoff: Daily cadence may not fit their life

purpose_lens.assumption: A daily offering can spare someone the decision of what to read without asking them to join a plan. A chosen plan adds a different commitment. A schedule can help coordinate that commitment. It can also ask for a rhythm that no longer fits their life. Before choosing the default, ask whether they need a shared date, a steady sequence or freedom to choose each time.
situations: Keep a shared date
Use a calendar when a group or season depends on reading together. Offer today’s passage and an independent catch-up route; changing one person’s schedule must not silently change everyone else’s.
Continue through a sequence
Resume at the next unread session when continuity matters more than dates. Explain that the sequence may no longer align with a shared calendar.
Choose freely each time
Offer a saved place or open library when the person does not want a plan. This preserves choice but gives them more decisions; optional suggestions can help without enrolling them.
purpose_lens.question: Is the reader returning for a practice they value, for useful support, or mainly to protect a reward? What evidence would help us distinguish these?
purpose_lens.test: Give participants a shared-date task and an interrupted personal sequence. Ask them to change pace, explain what moved, and find the next reading. Discuss usefulness and pressure separately from completion.
purpose_lens.guide_label: Reading plans and pressure

takeaway: Use a shared calendar when the date matters, or a sequence when continuing matters more than keeping up. Keep the saved place intact when the reader changes pace.

editorial_review.purpose: Someone wants reading structure that can adapt to their circumstances.
editorial_review.benefit: A chosen rhythm reduces repeated planning while preserving the option to pause or change pace.
editorial_review.drawback: Flexibility can make a shared calendar harder to coordinate. Multiple scheduling controls can also create complexity.
editorial_review.differences: A fixed date can support a group; irregular work or caring responsibilities may favour a sequence. Ask what structure helps rather than assigning a schedule from a user profile.
editorial_review.question: Does changing the rhythm preserve the person’s agency and the group’s expectations?
editorial_review.check: Pause a plan and reschedule it. Verify completed work, notes, reminder changes and group implications before confirmation.

title: Return without shame
summary: Make it easy to pick up a reading practice after time away.
problem: A comeback screen may frame absence as failure and discourage a meaningful new session.
solution: Show the saved place and a clear way to continue. In a dated plan, distinguish resuming from opening today’s reading. Make a different starting point available without erasing earlier work. Keep paused reminders paused unless the person chooses to restart them. A return should not require an explanation or a new commitment.
failure: A guilt message; demanding reasons for absence; “save your streak” payments; escalating reminder frequency after silence.
test: Compare returning-user experiences through interviews and longitudinal observation. Does the welcome respect choice rather than merely increase opens?

variants.tradeoff: Do not erase the saved place unnecessarily

purpose_lens.assumption: An absence tells us little about why someone left. The interface should not diagnose their motivation or require a renewed spiritual commitment before they can continue.
situations: Resume something chosen
Lead with the saved passage and intact notes. Show schedule changes neutrally rather than making the person reconstruct their place.
Join what is happening now
For a dated group practice, offer today’s reading with a separate route to earlier material. Do not mark skipped sessions complete.
Begin differently
Make changing or leaving a plan available. A short reading or audio option can help if chosen, but should not displace an explicit request to resume.
purpose_lens.question: Does the welcome serve the person’s next purpose, or mainly our wish to recover a lapsed user?
purpose_lens.test: Ask people to return after an interruption, resume or change direction, and explain the screen’s tone. Include people who choose not to restart. Do not require a reason for their absence.
purpose_lens.guide_label: Reading plans and pressure

takeaway: Begin with a useful next step: the saved passage, today’s group reading or a different starting point. Keep their notes and place; let the person choose what fits now.

editorial_review.purpose: Someone comes back after an interruption and wants a useful next step.
editorial_review.benefit: A neutral welcome and saved place can reduce the effort of returning.
editorial_review.drawback: Hiding all history may remove information someone values. A short suggested reading can distract from the person’s original plan.
editorial_review.differences: Some people want continuity; others want a fresh beginning. Absence may reflect illness, access barriers, dissatisfaction or simply a different priority—not a deficit to diagnose.
editorial_review.question: Can someone return without explaining their absence or making a new commitment?
editorial_review.check: Offer resume and a different starting point. Ask participants what the screen implies about their absence; do not infer comfort from increased opens.

title: Intent controls support the prompt
summary: Help people express scope through selections and task choices.
problem: A blank box makes users responsible for specifying passage, sources, purpose and output format in every prompt.
solution: Pair free text with editable context chips and concrete task controls. Use a passage selection, source scope and desired form to express intent. Confirm material assumptions rather than silently inferring them from private data.
failure: Forcing a complex prompt; invisible source filters; inferring belief or distress from a simple search.
test: Can novice users ask a scoped question and understand what sources and passage will be used? Test removing a context item and correcting an assumption.

variants.tradeoff: Context chips should be editable

variants.title: B · Editable scope
variants.caption: The active sources are visible and removable.
variants.when: The person wants to control source scope
variants.tradeoff: Removing a source must change retrieval transparently

variants.tradeoff: Clarify without turning the task into an interview

purpose_lens.assumption: Suggested actions define what the app considers worth asking. “Explain,” “compare” and “apply” privilege different purposes; none should silently become the goal of every conversation.
situations: Understand a passage
Start from the selected text and edition, with optional explanation or source lookup. Preserve a free-form question rather than making the reader choose a theological conclusion.
Prepare or investigate
Expose source scope and comparison controls. Let the person inspect disagreement and revise scope; do not make a devotional application mandatory.
Reflect personally
Offer an optional reflective prompt without assuming a disclosure is needed. Do not infer a person’s beliefs or emotional state from the selected passage.
purpose_lens.question: Can someone pursue a question the product did not anticipate, including one that challenges its preferred interpretation?
purpose_lens.test: Ask people to explain the active scope, remove a source, switch from explanation to comparison, and ask their own question. Check that the request and retrieval change with the controls, not just the visible labels.
purpose_lens.guide_label: AI, evidence and authority

takeaway: Pair free text with editable context chips and concrete task controls.

editorial_review.purpose: Someone knows the question but not how to write a detailed prompt.
editorial_review.benefit: Visible passage and source scope reduce repeated specification.
editorial_review.drawback: Defaults can narrow an answer in ways a reader does not notice.
editorial_review.differences: New users may benefit from a task suggestion; experienced users still need free text and removable context.
editorial_review.question: Which assumptions about sources and purpose are visible before sending?
editorial_review.check: Can novice users ask a scoped question and understand what sources and passage will be used? Test removing a context item and correcting an assumption.

title: A reference opens at a deliberate destination
summary: Choose the content scope, landing position and temporary cue separately.
problem: A link to Mark 1:8 can open the chapter at its beginning, land at verse 8, or display only verse 8. These choices support different tasks and should not be accidental.
solution: For contextual reading, open the containing chapter and place the first requested verse in view. For a focused preview, show only the verse or requested passage with a Read in context action. A chapter overview may open at the top, but retain the requested reference and provide Jump to verse. Scrolling and highlighting are independent: landing at a verse can use a temporary outline, a labelled margin cue, or no highlight. Mark a requested range rather than only its first verse when helpful. Temporary navigation cues never become saved annotations. Account for headers, players and delayed layout; retain back navigation to the search or chat.
failure: Opening at the chapter top without acknowledging the requested verse; permanently marking a deep-link target; hiding a focused excerpt’s boundaries; losing the origin.
test: Enter one verse, a range and a cross-chapter passage from search, chat and an external link. Check large text, cold loading, missing content and return navigation.

variants.title: A · Chapter overview
variants.caption: Opening at the top is explicit, with a route to the actual target.
variants.when: A chapter overview is the intended destination
variants.tradeoff: Retain the requested reference and a jump action

variants.title: B · Anchored chapter
variants.caption: The chapter remains available; the target is brought into view.

variants.tradeoff: A temporary navigation cue must not become a saved mark

editorial_review.purpose: Someone opens a reference from search, chat or an external link.
editorial_review.benefit: A deliberate landing point connects the requested reference to its surrounding text.
editorial_review.drawback: A focused excerpt can hide context; a chapter overview can make the requested verse hard to find. A cue may be mistaken for a saved highlight.
editorial_review.differences: A quick lookup benefits from immediate reference confirmation. A study task may need the whole argument. Large text, screen readers and slow loading change how the target must be revealed.
editorial_review.question: Does the destination fulfil the promise made by the link?
editorial_review.check: Open a single verse and a cross-chapter range after a cold start. Verify visible and accessible identification, no obscured target, and return to the origin.

title: Change translation without losing the passage
summary: Preserve a semantic reading anchor rather than a pixel offset.
problem: Different wording, poetry, headings and verse grouping change layout height. Retaining the old scroll offset can move the selected verse out of view.
solution: Before switching, identify the relevant anchor: the active selection or opened target, otherwise the visible reading verse; use the spoken verse only while Follow narration is enabled. Retain its approximate viewport position or bring it safely into view after the new edition has laid out. Reapply placement after late font or media loading only until the user scrolls; manual exploration takes precedence. Resolve versification with a trusted mapping and explain missing, split or merged verses. Keep reference notes separate from edition-specific word selections. Audio stays bound to its recorded edition: offer matching audio or clearly separate listening from the new text, and disable incompatible word cues.
failure: Restoring raw pixels; jumping to the chapter start; following audio after the reader scrolled away; copying word highlights onto unrelated wording; endlessly recentering during loading.
test: Switch editions while selecting a verse, freely reading, following audio, opening a note and using large text. Test poetry, missing verses, split or merged mappings, load failure and late reflow.

variants.tradeoff: Preserve the reading anchor rather than the audio anchor

editorial_review.purpose: A reader changes editions while keeping a passage in view.
editorial_review.benefit: A semantic anchor preserves the task despite changed text lengths.
editorial_review.drawback: Verse numbering or book availability may differ; a saved pixel offset cannot resolve this.
editorial_review.differences: A comparison task needs precise correspondence. Continuous reading needs a stable visible passage. Audio alignment may be unavailable in the new edition.
editorial_review.question: What should remain stable: the selected passage, the reading position or the playback position?
editorial_review.check: Change editions with large text, an active selection and unavailable audio. Explain missing references rather than silently substituting a nearby verse.

title: Chat contains source objects, not just bubbles
summary: Give verses, passages, links and media recognisable identity and appropriate actions.
problem: A bare link obscures its destination, while a large embed can crowd out the answer. Generated explanation can be mistaken for the text inside a Scripture card.
solution: Use an inline reference link for a brief citation, a bounded verse or passage card for text worth inspecting, and a full reader for sustained reading. Name edition, reference, visible range and source. Distinguish external link previews from Scripture and from generated commentary. Video cards identify publisher, duration and captions; audio cards retain passage and narrator. Do not autoplay. Provide plain links or labelled fallbacks when previews, media or permissions fail. Copy and sharing preserve reference and attribution where permitted. Returning from any destination restores conversation position.
failure: Autoplaying media; unlabelled generated verse text; enormous previews; a failed embed removing the source link; identical actions for read, play and external navigation.
test: Test a citation, single verse, long passage, external article, video and audio. Include blocked embeds, offline use, captions, large text, copy and return navigation.

Look closely at the wording

Explore a teaching resource
Show publisher, format and duration before opening an article or media item. A polished preview is not a quality endorsement; explain recommendation logic where it matters.

editorial_review.drawback: Large cards can dominate an answer; tiny links can conceal important context.

editorial_review.question: Is the object Scripture, interpretation or an external resource—and is that obvious?
editorial_review.check: Test a citation, single verse, long passage, external article, video and audio. Include blocked embeds, offline use, captions, large text, copy and return navigation.

title: Parallel reading chooses a useful arrangement
summary: Compare translations without forcing a desktop layout onto a small screen.
problem: Two adjacent translations can become narrow columns on a phone. Vertically stacked panes can hide the corresponding verse and make the relationship unclear.
solution: Choose left/right panes, top/bottom panes, or alternating edition blocks by the comparison task and available width. On mobile, a top/bottom split preserves line length, while a left/right split can suit brief passages when text remains readable. Offer a single-edition view or switching between editions when neither split fits enlarged text. On larger screens, side-by-side panes can support sustained comparison; let users resize or close panes without losing the reference. Keep edition labels, reference scope and scroll controls visible. Orientation names describe pane arrangement, not the direction in which Scripture should scroll.
failure: Shrinking text to fit columns; assuming landscape means enough space; hiding edition identity; putting one pane behind the player or keyboard.
test: Test portrait, landscape, a large screen, enlarged fonts, a long verse and poetry. Can users identify both editions, change arrangement and retain the target passage?

Study several passages at a desk

Return to devotional reading

editorial_review.purpose: A reader compares two editions or an edition with commentary.

editorial_review.drawback: Narrow columns and divided height can both impair reading.
editorial_review.differences: A phone with enlarged text may need sequential switching even when a large screen can show adjacent panes.
editorial_review.question: Does simultaneous visibility help enough to justify the lost reading space?
editorial_review.check: Test portrait, landscape, a large screen, enlarged fonts, a long verse and poetry. Can users identify both editions, change arrangement and retain the target passage?

title: Linked scrolling follows passage identity
summary: Let parallel panes move together or independently, with an explicit way to rejoin.
problem: Different wording and poetry create different heights. Equal pixel scrolling can show unrelated verses in adjacent panes.
solution: Offer linked and independent scrolling. In linked mode, map the leading pane’s visible verse or passage anchor into the other pane instead of copying pixel offsets. Keep a stable leading pane during an interaction; avoid feedback loops and jitter. In independent mode, show each reference and offer Align at this verse. Rejoining uses the user’s chosen pane as the anchor. If a mapping is missing, split or merged, explain the correspondence and avoid pretending an exact line alignment. Playback following is a separate control; specify which pane it follows.
failure: Proportional scrolling presented as exact correspondence; snapping back after exploration; both panes endlessly steering each other; silently changing playback.
test: Scroll either pane, unlink, explore another chapter and rejoin. Test poetry, verse bridges, missing mappings, touch gestures, resizing and audio following.

editorial_review.drawback: Automatic alignment can disrupt independent exploration or fail with different numbering.
editorial_review.differences: Close comparison may favour linked panes; a cross-reference investigation may need independent positions.

title: Group editions around a shared verse
summary: Use repeated verse groups when matching corresponding passages matters more than continuous reading.
problem: Independent columns make a short comparison difficult when translation lengths differ. Interleaving every verse can fragment a sustained reading task.
solution: Group the chosen editions beneath a common reference. Repeat edition labels and preserve wording, paragraph structure and edition-specific numbering. Offer stacked edition blocks for narrow screens and columns inside each verse group where width permits. A continuous-text alternative supports reading an argument or poem. With many editions, let users choose which to include rather than endlessly expanding every group. Explain split, merged or missing verse mappings within the group.
failure: Aligning words just because verse numbers match; stripping poetic structure; hiding edition labels after the first group; substituting empty text for a missing verse.
test: Compare short and long verses, poetry, two and several editions, different numbering and large text. Can readers switch back to continuous context?

editorial_review.purpose: Someone wants to compare the wording of corresponding verses.
editorial_review.benefit: Edition blocks grouped under one reference make correspondence easier to inspect.
editorial_review.drawback: Interleaving can fragment poetry and an extended argument.
editorial_review.differences: A short comparison may suit grouped blocks; sustained reading needs continuous context.
editorial_review.question: Are we helping comparison without implying word-for-word equivalence?

title: Interlinear rows expose their alignment
summary: Distinguish source-language tokens, glosses and translation wording.
problem: An interlinear view can make a gloss look like a complete translation and imply one-to-one word equivalence. Dense lexical metadata can overwhelm the passage.
solution: Label the source text, token alignment, gloss source and reading direction. A gloss is a lexical aid rather than a fluent translation or a definitive meaning in context. Offer compact token stacks, expandable word detail and wider aligned rows where space permits. Let the user choose which rows to display: original script, transliteration, gloss, morphology or lexical reference. On mobile, wrap whole token groups in source order or open one token at a time; preserve right-to-left ordering and bidirectional labels. Distinguish source-order interlinear from translation-order reverse interlinear. Missing token links need an explicit unavailable state rather than invented alignment.

failure: Clipping a passage without notice; treating one boundary as universal across editions; replacing source text with an AI summary; making context available only through chat.

title: Citations in AI answers

failure: Whole-answer citation lists with unclear claim mapping; invented sources or timestamps; counting repeated sources as independent support; inaccessible evidence presented as verified.

title: Identify what AI did, where it matters
summary: Label the actor, action and artifact at the moment they could be misunderstood.
problem: A Bible app mixes verified Scripture, authored commentary, personal notes and generated material. A brand name or sparkle icon may leave readers unsure whether they are reading a translation, a pastor’s words or an AI explanation.

title: Paragraphs or one verse per line?

failure: Flattening poetry into prose; treating verse breaks as sentence boundaries; changing layout and losing the selected passage.
test: Compare sustained reading and reference lookup at large text sizes. Ask readers to locate a verse, change layout and explain where the paragraph ends.
faith: Neither layout is inherently more faithful. The task, source structure and reader’s preferences matter.

title: How do readers move to the next chapter?
summary: Compare continuous reading, explicit buttons and a persistent navigation bar.
problem: No visible navigation can make a chapter feel like a dead end. Persistent controls consume space and can compete with audio, selection tools or the keyboard.
solution: Match navigation to the current task, not a permanent reader category. Continuous reading can cross a visible chapter boundary without permanent arrows. Discrete chapters benefit from explicit previous and next destinations. A compact bar suits frequent movement, while study may additionally need a back trail, saved place and direct reference entry. A bounded passage can end without a prominent Next action; retain optional wider context where useful. Keep controls clear of the final lines, audio controls and selection tools.
failure: Swipe-only navigation; wrapping from the last book to the first without warning; hiding the last verse behind a bar; changing chapter during text selection; a missing download leaving a blank page.
test: Give participants different tasks: continue a narrative, compare distant references, follow a spoken reference, resume a note and finish one shared passage. Observe misnavigation, return to place and unwanted interruptions. Ask whether they wanted a next step; do not infer usefulness from the number of chapters opened. Include large text, assistive technology and unavailable chapters.
faith: A product can invite exploration without implying that more reading proves greater faithfulness. Consider whether this particular invitation supports the person’s practice or primarily serves an engagement target.
flow: Identify the current chapter and the available next destination.
On a deliberate change, preserve the old position for back navigation.

problem: The same query can name a book, quote wording or ask a question. A fluent inline answer may look as certain as an exact reference match even when it is generated.

title: Orient within a liturgical calendar
summary: Make the tradition, date and observance clear before offering readings or prayer.
takeaway: Start with today in the selected calendar. Keep its tradition and region discoverable, and offer a date list or season view for people preparing ahead. A shared observance is not a personal completion deadline.
problem: A generic “today’s readings” label can hide which calendar, locality or service supplied them. A month grid alone may show dates without helping someone understand the season or find the right office.
solution: Name the calendar and jurisdiction, service or office, civil date and source. Persist an explicitly chosen calendar without inferring belief from location. Separate browsing another date from changing today. Use authoritative calendar data and review tradition-specific rules for transfers, precedence, optional observances and evening boundaries. If a source offers alternatives, name them rather than silently choosing. Cache a versioned date range and disclose unavailable or stale data.
failure: Treating one tradition’s calendar as universal; silently switching calendars on travel; substituting ordinary readings for an unavailable observance; using liturgical colour as the only identifier; showing missed feasts as overdue tasks.
test: Check representative movable and fixed observances, competing observances and year boundaries against the named authority. Test a date link while travelling, offline access outside the cached range, large text and return to today. Have a knowledgeable reviewer verify the supported tradition and locale.
faith: A calendar invites participation in a received communal rhythm. It can offer continuity and introduce unfamiliar texts without asking each person to curate a daily selection. Preserve that context rather than reducing a season to a campaign or completion challenge. Different traditions and local calendars need explicit treatment.

title: Make room for prayer
summary: Compare a prayer text, a guided sequence and a quiet space without requiring personal input.
takeaway: Choose the surface around the prayer practice: a readable order for set prayer, gentle steps for guided reflection, or minimal controls for silence. Writing, recording and sharing should be separate choices.
problem: A chat box or journal can imply that prayer must be typed, answered or saved. A timer can suggest performance; a prayer list can expose other people’s personal circumstances.
solution: Identify the prayer’s source, author or tradition and any adaptation. For set forms, keep instructions and responses distinguishable, with adjustable text and optional audio. For guidance, show an outline and let people pause without requiring written answers. For silence, offer an optional timer or end cue with a complete untimed route. Request lists and journals are separate, optional functions with explicit storage, deletion and sharing rules. Playback should not activate a microphone; generated wording requires clear provenance and review before saving or sharing.
failure: Requiring a typed prayer to continue; claiming an AI response speaks for God; marking a request answered automatically; treating minutes or taps as prayer quality; uploading dictated prayer without clear choice; exposing a request on a lock screen.
test: Pray from a set text at large type, pause a guided sequence, and finish a silent session with no timer. Confirm that no recording or entry is required. If journalling is offered, test save, discard, deletion and audience understanding with synthetic content.
faith: Some people pray with received words, others with their own words or in silence. The interface should be honest about the practice it supports. A completed audio file is a playback event; the app cannot determine whether a person prayed well or whether a prayer was answered.

title: How human should the assistant appear?
summary: Choose social cues deliberately, from names and avatars to typing dots, voice and claims of presence.
takeaway: Use warmth to make the interaction approachable; make the system’s identity and actual activity equally clear.
problem: A face, personal name, intimate language and typing indicator can together suggest a human relationship or pastoral presence, even when a small AI label is technically visible.
solution: Review the whole combination of cues. A descriptive AI role is a useful starting point; a named persona needs equally clear AI identification. Friendly first-person language can make conversation understandable, but avoid fabricated feelings, lived experience, clergy credentials or personal spiritual authority. During waits, describe actual system activity. Dots can be a compact response-pending cue under an AI sender label; do not label them as a human typing or add delays purely to simulate a person. Keep stop, retry and real handoff states clear.
failure: A human portrait with a buried AI label; “I have been praying for you”; invented human typing, read receipts or online availability; claims of personal attachment; status text claiming sources were checked when no retrieval occurred; a fake human support handoff.
test: Show the entry, a wait state and a response without explaining them. Ask who is responding, what the system is doing, what it remembers and whether a real person is available. Repeat after voice use and with people of different AI familiarity. Check cancellation, reduced motion and screen-reader announcements.
faith: Hospitality can shape the tone without simulating pastoral accountability or divine authority. A tool can help someone draft a prayer, reflect or prepare for a human conversation. Whether it is framed as a companion deserves explicit theological and safeguarding reflection, rather than being inherited from a retention strategy.

title: Explain AI, fallibility and privacy where they matter
summary: Layer chat disclosures across entry, composer, response and sharing instead of relying on one disclaimer.
takeaway: Keep AI identity visible; put specific limitations and data-use information beside the decisions they affect.
problem: A footer may be overlooked, onboarding may be forgotten, and a copied response may lose its AI label. A generic error warning also says nothing about who receives a personal message.
solution: Use a concise entry explanation and persistent AI sender identity. Keep an accessible privacy route near the composer, with a short just-in-time explanation before a new kind of collection, upload or memory use. Describe actual processing, access and retention; do not invent privacy assurances. Put task-specific limitations beside the answer and offer checking or correction actions. Keep Scripture attribution separate from generated explanation, and carry meaningful origin labels into saved and shared outputs.
failure: Legal text only in settings; “AI may be wrong” used to excuse unchecked quotations; blanket confidential or anonymous claims; a warning shown only after sending; repeating a large banner on every answer; treating a privacy link or ordinary Send action as blanket consent.
test: Enter chat through a deep link, inspect who responds, open privacy information without losing the draft, add a file and share an answer. Ask what leaves the device, who may access it and how to check a claim. Test long conversations, screen readers and error states.
faith: An intimate prayer or confession can be entrusted to a product more readily than its data practices justify. Clarity is part of care. A warning should support a meaningful choice, not place responsibility for every failure on a vulnerable reader.

title: Actions on AI answers
summary: Copy, share, save, listen, try again, simplify, branch, check quotations, rate or report: choose the actions an AI answer needs and make each one honest about what it does.
takeaway: Offer the few actions people need most, keep the rest one step away, and let every action carry the answer’s origin and say what happens to the data.
problem: General AI apps such as Gemini, ChatGPT and Claude put many actions under every answer, from copy and read aloud to try again, double-check, branch and report legal issue. Each one makes a promise: that a copy keeps its label, that feedback goes somewhere, that “thinking” is what the model did. Unlabelled icons are hard to understand, and in a Bible app a shared answer can be mistaken for Scripture or a pastor’s words.
solution: Decide which actions this product needs. Keep two or three visible and put the rest behind “More”. Copy and share carry the AI label and references; saving to notes keeps AI answers apart from the reader’s own words; feedback says who sees it and whether it trains models; try again and simpler versions keep the original and let people compare, because regenerating until a preferred doctrinal answer appears is a real risk; checking quotations compares every quotation with the edition; “what the assistant did” lists real operations rather than private reasoning; reporting routes to a person with a stated response time. Consider putting actions on the Scripture objects instead, so the passage, not the generated text, is what travels.
failure: Icon-only rows without accessible names; a copy that drops the AI label; thumbs that silently feed training; “thinking” presented as proof of correctness; a report button with no stated owner; sharing generated interpretation as if it were Scripture.
test: Ask people to say what each icon does before tapping it. Copy and share an answer and check what the recipient sees. Rate an answer and ask who they think will read the rating. Compare a full row with three actions plus “More” for findability and errors.
faith: What travels beyond the conversation matters. A shared answer may be read as Scripture, as the church’s teaching or as a friend’s counsel. Letting the passage, rather than the generated text, be the thing people save and share keeps the Bible and its interpretation distinct.

title: How much text at once
summary: One word, one verse, one verse in focus with its context, one passage or a whole chapter: choose the unit of Scripture a reading screen asks someone to hold, and let them move along the spectrum.
takeaway: Match the unit to the reading: smaller for meditation, memory and read-along, a passage for daily reading and study, longer for narrative and argument. Keep context one step away and the reader’s place across modes.
problem: People read on phones in shorter, more selective sessions, and many Bible apps now offer verse cards, focus modes, read-along highlighting or speed readers. Each sets how much text someone sees at once. A single verse is easy to start and easy to lift out of context; a whole chapter keeps the argument but can feel like a wall on a small screen.
solution: Decide which reading this screen serves. For meditation or memory, show a verse at a time or a verse in focus with the passage dimmed around it. For listening, move the focus with the audio. For a daily reading, show one passage with its reference, what comes before and after, and a way into the chapter. For a book read through, offer calm long-form text. Keep the same place when someone changes mode, and never strand a verse without a route to its context.
failure: A verse shown alone with no way to its chapter; a box to tick on every verse that turns a passage into a to-do list, or ticks verses merely opened; editorial headings presented as Scripture; word-by-word display used for study; auto-advancing text with no pause or rewind; focus modes that hide the text from screen readers; losing the reader’s place when switching modes.
test: Ask people to read the same passage in two modes, then retell it and answer a question that depends on the verse before. Time how long it takes to find the context of a single verse. Test focus and read-along with screen readers, reduced motion and people with dyslexia or attention difficulties.
faith: Verse numbers date from the sixteenth century and chapter divisions from the thirteenth; neither is part of the inspired text, and both make it easy to read a sentence apart from its argument. Smaller units also have a long devotional history: lectio divina dwells on a few verses read slowly and repeatedly. The question is not which unit is more spiritual, but whether the screen keeps the verse connected to the passage it belongs to.

title: Numbers, headings and notes
summary: From a reader’s edition with nothing but the words, through verse numbers, section titles and note markers, to a full study layout: decide what sits around Scripture, who wrote it, and who can switch it off.
takeaway: Default to what the main reading needs, mark every addition as an addition, keep notes one tap away without losing the place, and let readers change it.
problem: Almost nothing around the biblical text is part of it. Verse numbers, chapter breaks, section titles, red letters, footnotes, cross-references and study notes were added by printers, translators and editors over centuries. Each helps someone find, follow or understand; each also shapes how the text is read and can be mistaken for Scripture itself.
solution: Choose a default by the main reading the product serves: a reader’s edition for reading through, numbers and titles for finding and following, notes and study material for study. Make every addition look like an addition: lighter type for numbers, a different style for titles, markers that open notes in a sheet and return to the same verse. Say who wrote headings and notes. Offer a settings drawer that changes the apparatus without moving the reader’s place, and keep poetry lineation and paragraphing from the edition.
failure: Headings styled like Scripture; study notes that read as the text’s own voice; note markers too small to tap or that jump away from the passage; settings that reflow and lose the reader’s place; red letters or headings that cannot be switched off; verse-per-line layouts that break poetry and paragraphs.
test: Ask readers which parts of the screen are Scripture and which were added. Open a note and return: does the reader land on the same verse? Switch settings mid-chapter and check the place is kept. Compare retelling after reading the same passage as a reader’s edition and as a study layout.
faith: Traditions disagree about apparatus. King James forbade marginal notes because the Geneva notes argued politics and theology; the Scofield notes later carried a whole system of interpretation to millions of readers. Reader’s editions remove everything so the books can be read whole. None of these is neutral: what surrounds the text quietly teaches people how to read it.

title: Bible audio
summary: From text alone, through a listen button and read-along, to audio built for a dark screen and fully produced devotionals: decide how much the voice leads, whose voice it is, and how a listening session ends.
takeaway: Treat listening as reading, say whose voice it is, let the text follow the voice when the screen is on, keep sessions working with the screen off, and end in quiet rather than autoplay.
problem: Scripture was heard long before it was read silently, and for many people today listening is the main or only way in. Apps offer a play button, highlighted read-along, full players for commuting and sleep, and produced devotionals with music, reflection and silence. Each decides how much the voice leads, whether the voice is a person or a machine, and what happens when the reading ends.
solution: Offer audio wherever the text is, and say whose voice it is: a named narrator, or a clearly labelled synthetic voice. When the screen is on, let the text follow the voice at verse or sentence level, with pause and rewind. Build a full player that works with the screen off, with skip, speed and a sleep timer that stops at the end of a passage. In produced devotionals, name who wrote the reflections, keep Scripture distinct from commentary, make music optional, and end with silence or a choice rather than the next track.
failure: Unlabelled synthetic voices; voices that imitate a known pastor without consent; autoplay that runs into the next chapter or an advert; read-along that cannot be paused; music that cannot be turned off; reflections that sound like Scripture; audio that stops when the screen locks.
test: Ask listeners whether a voice is human or synthetic and how they know. Listen on a commute with the screen off and check skip, pause and sleep. Compare recall of a passage heard with and without music. Test read-along with screen readers and people with dyslexia.
faith: “Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17). Scripture was written to be read aloud: “Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear” (Revelation 1:3). A voice is not neutral: tone, pace and emphasis interpret, as a reader in church does. Whose voice reads Scripture, and whether it is a person at all, is a question of trust as well as design.

title: AI persona
summary: From a plain tool with no name, through labelled and named assistants, to personas, companions and chatbots speaking as Jesus: decide how much personhood an AI in a faith app performs, and make what it is as clear as how it sounds.
takeaway: Be warm without pretending to be a person: label the AI wherever it speaks, never claim to pray, feel or be always there, describe what it is really doing while it waits, let people leave, and never generate words in God’s or Christ’s voice.
problem: People treat computers as social actors, and a name, a face, typing dots, a first-person voice and memory together suggest someone is there. In a faith app that someone can seem to be a friend who prays, a pastor, or Christ himself. Faith apps now offer named personas, companions available “24/7” and character chats with biblical figures, often to people who are lonely, frightened or grieving.
solution: Choose the register on purpose. Start from a labelled assistant: an AI mark beside every reply, a kind voice, and a status line that describes what the system is actually doing. If you give it a name, let it say in its own voice what it cannot do: pray, keep a confidence the way a pastor does, or be present. Keep disclosure where decisions happen: at entry, at the composer, beside answers and on anything shared. Avoid claims of feelings, prayer or constant availability; let people leave without guilt; route to people for pastoral care. Do not generate first-person speech for God, Jesus or other biblical figures.
failure: A portrait and a personal name with a buried AI label; “I’ve been praying for you”; “I’m always here for you”; typing dots labelled as a person typing; farewells that guilt people into staying; a voice call that implies someone on the line; memory used to simulate concern; a chatbot speaking as Jesus and promising outcomes; disclosure only in the terms of service.
test: Show the entry, a wait and a reply without explanation, and ask who is responding, what it is doing and whether it can pray for them. Say goodbye and note what happens. Test with people who are lonely or grieving (with care), with teenagers where permitted, and after voice use. Ask pastors and theologians to review persona and character copy.
faith: Presence is at the heart of Christian faith: “the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14), and the church gathers in body (Hebrews 10:25). A tool can help someone find words for prayer or prepare for a conversation, but it cannot pray, keep vigil or carry another’s burden (Galatians 6:2). Scripture is severe about speaking in God’s name without being sent (Deuteronomy 18:20; Jeremiah 23:16). The Vatican’s Antiqua et nova calls AI “a tool, not a person”; misrepresenting it as one should always be avoided.

title: Translations
summary: From one translation chosen with enough context, through switching in place and verse-by-verse comparison, to parallel panes and the Greek or Hebrew under every word: decide how much of translation’s variety a reader sees, and keep them on the same verse while they look.
takeaway: Help people choose a translation with its approach in view; keep the selected verse as the anchor when they switch; compare verse by verse for wording and in linked panes for reading; and treat interlinear glosses as word aids, never as the meaning.
problem: Every translation is an interpretation, and readers rarely know how theirs was made. A list of abbreviations hides the choice; switching can lose the place; two columns on a phone become unreadably narrow; panes scrolled by pixels drift onto different verses; and an interlinear gloss can look like the “real” meaning of a word.
solution: Show full names, approach and date when people choose, and say which translations are available offline or with audio. When switching, keep the selected or visible verse in place. For checking wording, group translations under each verse and mark what differs. For reading two texts, use full-width panes stacked on a phone, linked by verse with a clear way to unlink and realign. Offer interlinear for study, with each row named, glosses labelled as word aids, and word detail that shows how translations render a word. Respect licensing and versification.
failure: Abbreviation-only lists; switching that jumps to the chapter start; side-by-side columns of 20 characters on a phone; panes linked by scroll position; marking every reordered word as different; glosses presented as the meaning; Greek or Hebrew without a language tag or right-to-left support; quoting licensed translations beyond their limits.
test: Ask readers to explain the difference between two translations they chose. Switch with a verse selected, while reading and while listening, and check the place is kept. Compare a verse in each layout at 200% text size. Ask readers what a gloss means, and whether it is “the real meaning”. Test Hebrew with right-to-left reading and a screen reader.
faith: Christianity has always been read in translation: the New Testament quotes the Greek Septuagint, and at Pentecost “each one heard them speaking his own language” (Acts 2:6). The 1611 translators, quoting Augustine, held that variety of translations helps readers find the sense of Scripture. Lamin Sanneh argued that translatability is at the heart of Christian mission: no language is too common for the word of God. Comparing translations is an old discipline, not a sign of doubt.

title: Highlights and notes
summary: From a bookmark that only says “return here”, through highlights and labelled marks, to private notes and notes shared with a group or the public: decide how much a mark says, who can see it, and what happens to it in another translation.
takeaway: Make marking one tap with undo; distinguish marks by shape as well as colour and keep them apart from selection and playback; attach notes to the verse and highlights to their translation; keep notes private by default; and show exactly who will see a shared note before it is shared.
problem: Readers mark Scripture to return, to remember, to ask, and to talk with others. Apps offer colour palettes, notebooks, tags and public notes, often before the reader has finished the thought. Colour-only marks fail some readers and collide with selection and read-along highlighting; marks on exact words break when the translation changes; and notes on Scripture can reveal faith, doubt and private struggles to people they were never meant for.
solution: Offer a small menu over the selection with one-tap marking and undo; leave labels and organisation for later. Give each kind of mark its own shape, and keep selection, search and playback cues visibly different from saved marks. Attach highlights to the exact words in their translation and say so elsewhere; attach bookmarks and notes to the verse so they follow any translation. Keep notes private by default and treat them as sensitive data. Make sharing a separate step that names the audience and previews what they will see; label other readers’ notes as theirs and let people turn them off.
failure: A colour picker before every highlight; colour as the only difference between marks; read-along highlighting that looks like a saved mark; highlights silently lost or moved onto different words after switching translation; notes public by default; a “share” that publishes to everyone; others’ notes styled like study notes; inferring mood or belief from marks for analytics.
test: Mark, undo and re-mark a phrase; repeat with a screen reader and in greyscale. Switch translation and ask where each mark went and why. Play audio over marked verses. Ask people who can see a note they just shared, and compare with the truth.
faith: Scripture asks to be kept, not only read: “Write them on the doorposts of your houses” (Deuteronomy 6:9); “I have hidden Your word in my heart” (Psalm 119:11); Mary “treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart” (Luke 2:19). Christians have long read with a pen: Jonathan Edwards filled an interleaved Bible with over five thousand notes across three decades. A mark is often a prayer or a question, and belongs to the reader.

title: Study helps
summary: From a preview card under the verse, through a sheet and a study panel, to a page of its own or help only on request: decide where commentary, cross-references and sermon clips open, how readers find them, and how they get back to the verse.
takeaway: Keep the verse in view while help is open, or bring the reader back to it; mark resources quietly and let readers switch markers off; name every author, date and kind of resource; say whether a panel follows the reading or stays put; and give media a transcript, captions and its place in the whole.
problem: Bible apps attach commentaries, study notes, cross-references, videos and sermon clips to verses. Where that help opens decides whether it supports reading or replaces it. A full-screen resource loses the place; a panel that silently changes under the reader confuses; markers on every verse turn Scripture into a menu; a commentary without an author reads like the Bible’s own voice; and a short sermon clip can say something its speaker did not mean in context.
solution: Start with a short preview anchored to the verse, with the full resource one tap away. For longer help, use a sheet that leaves the verse visible, or a study panel on larger screens, and say whether the panel follows the reading or is pinned. If help takes the whole screen, make Back return to the same verse and show it. Mark verses with resources quietly, and let readers turn markers off. Show the kind of resource, its author and date, and where several voices disagree, show more than one. For media, show where the clip sits in the whole, offer what came before, and provide captions and a corrected transcript.
failure: A commentary styled like Scripture; no author or date; markers on every verse; autoplaying video between verses; a panel that changes without saying so; Back that returns to the top of the chapter; a 30-second clip presented as the speaker’s whole view; automatic transcripts quoted uncorrected; locked resources shown as if available.
test: Ask readers to open help on a verse, read it and return; note whether they are on the same verse. Ask who wrote the help and when. Scroll with a following panel and ask why it changed. Watch a clip, then the two minutes before, and ask whether the meaning changed. Test with captions, a screen reader and 200% text.
faith: Scripture itself shows readers helped beside the text: the Levites “read from the Book of the Law of God, explaining it and giving insight, so that the people could understand what was being read” (Nehemiah 8:8), and the Ethiopian asked, “How can I … unless someone guides me?” (Acts 8:31). The medieval Glossa Ordinaria set the text in the centre of the page and the commentary around it, in a smaller hand. The King James translators allowed no interpretive notes in the margin, only notes on words and cross-references, because the Geneva Bible’s notes were thought partisan. Where help sits, and whose voice it carries, has always been a theological question as well as a layout one.

title: Reading plans
summary: From a plan tied to calendar dates, through a sequence that waits for the reader and a weekly rhythm, to readings that belong to each day, and streaks as a warning case: decide what a plan asks of time, and what happens when someone comes back after days away.
takeaway: Choose dates only when reading together on the same day matters; otherwise let the plan wait. Never turn missed days into a debt: welcome people back with a choice of where to start, keep their place and notes, let them move dates, change pace or pause, and do not make a streak the point.
problem: Reading plans promise structure, and most tie each reading to a date. When life interrupts, the days pile up: “9 days behind”, a broken streak, a plan that now ends weeks late. People who feel they have failed often stop altogether, and some apps sell a way to repair the streak. Yet shared dates are also what let a church or small group read together.
solution: Decide what the plan is for. For reading together, keep shared dates but treat open days as available, not overdue, and on return offer today’s reading, where they stopped, or moving their own dates. For personal reading, use a sequence that waits, or a weekly number that starts fresh. For daily texts, let each day stand on its own. Explain what each change will do before it happens, keep completed readings and notes, let people pause without reminders, and say nothing about absence beyond what helps them choose.
failure: “You are 9 days behind”; a catch-up list of every missed reading; streak counters on the home screen; streak repair for money or gems; reminders that escalate after silence; resetting the plan and erasing history; group dashboards that show who is behind; asking why someone was away.
test: Ask people returning after a week, a month and a year what they would do next and how the screen makes them feel. Try each change (pause, move dates, own pace) and ask what will happen before confirming. Test with a group plan: can someone fall back without the group seeing it?
faith: Christians have long read Scripture by rule and by calendar: the daily office, lectionaries and the Moravian watchwords give each day its texts. Rules served the reader. Benedict asked that the whole psalter be prayed each week, yet told anyone who found his arrangement unsatisfactory to arrange whatever he judged better. Robert Murray M’Cheyne, whose 1842 calendar is still widely used, warned that it might become “a yoke too heavy to bear”: “throw aside the fetter, and feed at liberty in the sweet garden of God.” His mercies are “new every morning” (Lamentations 3:22–23); a plan should be too.

title: Prayer
summary: From the received words of a church’s daily office, through guided steps and a list of people to pray for, to quiet prayer with nothing to fill in, and counted prayer as a warning case: decide what each surface asks someone to read, type, share or count.
takeaway: Name the tradition, calendar and author of every prayer; tell instructions, responses and silence apart; let people pause and finish without typing anything; keep prayer requests private by default and show exactly who will see a shared one, and for how long; let silence end without a score; and never turn prayer into minutes, streaks or public totals.
problem: Prayer apps offer daily offices, guided sessions, intention lists, timers and community request feeds. Each control says what counts as prayer: an empty field asks for words, a timer for duration, a checkmark for completion, a counter for volume. A generic “today” can hide whose calendar supplied the readings. Prayer requests name illnesses, families and doubts, and religious belief is special-category data. Some apps count minutes and streaks, show billions of “prayers prayed”, and let friends remind each other to keep up.
solution: Decide which practice the surface serves. For set prayer, show the order with its source and calendar, keep rubrics, the leader’s lines and the people’s responses visibly different, and let people look ahead without changing today. For guided prayer, show the outline, let people move at their own pace and keep any note optional and private. For people someone prays for, store requests on the device by default; for groups, name the audience and an end date before anything is shared, and ask before sharing someone else’s story. For silence, offer a complete untimed route and an optional end bell. Record nothing about prayer that the person did not choose to keep.
failure: A generic “today’s prayer” with no tradition named; a confession and its rubric in the same type; steps that advance by themselves; a required text field before continuing; prayer requests public by default or shown on the lock screen; marking a request “answered” automatically; minutes prayed, streaks and global totals; “Remind” buttons for friends who missed a day; sharing “I prayed 14 minutes” to social media; selling prayer data to advertisers.
test: Pray each surface without typing, recording or sharing anything, and ask what the app expected of you. Ask people to tell a response from an instruction in the office, and to name the calendar. Add a request for a group and ask who will see it and until when. Sit in silence with and without a timer. Check what is stored and sent with a network inspector.
faith: Jesus told his disciples to pray to the Father “who is unseen”, not “to be seen by men”, and warned against thinking “that by their many words they will be heard” (Matthew 6:5–7); when they asked, “Lord, teach us to pray”, he gave them words (Luke 11:1–4). The early church “devoted themselves … to prayer” together (Acts 2:42), and the Spirit helps “with groans too deep for words” when we do not know what to pray (Romans 8:26). Received words, one’s own words and silence all belong to Christian prayer. Benedict wrote that “we are heard not for our many words but for our purity of heart”, and asked that prayer be “short and pure”. An app cannot tell whether someone prayed, and should not pretend to count it.

title: Devotional audio
summary: From guided prayer with Scripture read twice and room for silence, through a teaching conversation and a one-voice devotional talk, to a sleep story that fades out, and an endless generated stream as a warning case: decide what each format does with Scripture, with the listener’s attention, and with the end of the session.
takeaway: Choose the format for the listener’s moment, not for listening time. Read Scripture whole and name who reads it; separate the reading from commentary; leave real silence, and in prayer let it wait for the listener; name every author, host and musician; and let every session end, with nothing queued after it.
problem: Devotional audio has become a crowded genre: guided prayer apps, Bible-teaching podcasts, morning devotionals, sleep stories and now AI-generated daily episodes. Each shapes how Scripture is heard: how much of it, by whom, framed by what. Hosts become familiar voices that listeners trust like friends. Players borrowed from podcast and video apps autoplay the next episode, and generated audio can be produced without end, often without a named author.
solution: Name the format and its purpose before playback. For prayer, read Scripture whole, often twice, separate reflection from reading, and leave silence that can wait. For teaching, name sources and distinguish the text from the hosts’ interpretation. For a talk, keep the passage at the centre and the host’s story in service of it. For sleep, fade to silence and play nothing after. Credit voices, authors and music, label synthetic voices, and end every session.
failure: Scripture read in fragments beneath music; commentary that sounds like the text; silence cut to keep attention; hosts presented as friends who know the listener; autoplay into the next episode; sleep content followed by more content; generated episodes without an author; “never run out” offers; streaks for listening.
test: Ask listeners after a session what the passage said and what the host said, and whether they could tell them apart. Time the silences. Check what plays after the session ends. Ask who wrote and who read each part, and whether any voice was synthetic.
faith: “Faith comes by hearing” (Romans 10:17), and the church has always shaped how Scripture is heard: read, sung, preached, prayed. Ezra’s Levites read the Law, “explaining it and giving insight, so that the people could understand what was being read” (Nehemiah 8:8), keeping the reading and the explanation distinct. “I will lie down and sleep in peace” (Psalm 4:8). And the prophet asks, “Why spend … your labor on that which does not satisfy?” (Isaiah 55:2). Devotional audio can serve all of these, or replace them with endless listening.
