title: Check-ins and assessments
summary: From a few setup questions that only shape what the app suggests, through a daily check-in, a gifts inventory and a church survey, to a spiritual score as a warning case: decide what each question is for, what is kept, who sees a result, and how much the result claims to know.
takeaway: Ask only what changes what the app offers, say what each answer changes, and let every question be skipped. Treat feelings and faith as special-category data: keep answers on the device by default, let people delete them, and share nothing automatically. Present results as starting points for trying and for conversation with people who know the person, never as a grade, a stage or a rank.
problem: Christian apps increasingly ask before they give: onboarding quizzes about goals and Bible familiarity, daily mood check-ins “with myself, with others, with God”, long personality tests that produce a “spiritual health report”. Churches have done something similar for decades with spiritual gifts inventories, Natural Church Development surveys and Willow Creek’s Reveal study. Asking can help: naming a feeling, finding a place to serve, a church hearing its members. But answers about mood and faith are intimate and legally protected, onboarding quizzes often serve a paywall, and a number can start to stand for a life with God.
solution: Name the purpose of each question set. For personalisation, ask few questions, say what each changes, allow skipping and editing, and ask nothing about health or belief that the app does not need. For a check-in, let naming be enough, respond with Scripture or a next step rather than a score, and keep the record on the device with a delete option. For gifts, frame results as places to try and people to talk with. For a church survey, keep answers anonymous and aggregated, and share results as a conversation starter. Never send anything automatically, and never rank people.
failure: Quizzes that cannot be skipped and end in a paywall; questions about anxiety, sins or shame without saying why; mood records sent to servers or friends automatically; charts of feelings that invite self-monitoring; results that hand out a label (“You are a Teacher”); spiritual scores, stages and rankings against others; prompts to retake a test to raise a score; leaders seeing individual answers.
test: For every question, ask what it changes and who could ever see the answer, and check that it can be skipped. Ask people to read their result aloud and say what it claims about them, and whether that is fair. Check what is stored and sent with a network inspector. Ask a pastor or spiritual director how they would respond to the same answers.
faith: Self-examination is old Christian practice. “Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith” (2 Corinthians 13:5); “Search me, O God, and know my heart” (Psalm 139:23). The Examen asks people to notice their feelings each evening, and Wesley’s band meetings asked the same questions every week, among friends. Paul wrote that “to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good” (1 Corinthians 12:7), and told readers, “Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought” (Romans 12:3). He also wrote “I do not even judge myself … It is the Lord who judges me” (1 Corinthians 4:3–4). Asking can serve discernment; only God knows a heart, and no app should pretend to score one.

status: Research-informed design proposal · draft for review
title: Sharing with a group
summary: From a request kept between someone and God, through one listener they choose, a few friends and a group with a leader, to the whole church and a public wall, with a board ranked by prayer streaks as a warning case: decide who hears a request, what each listener can and must do with it, and what comes back.
takeaway: Show who will hear a request, for how long, before anything is written; ask before naming anyone else; say before someone shares that some listeners have to pass concerns on; when a church sets the app up, name its safeguarding contact, someone outside the leadership a concern might be about; keep an independent route beside the church’s; help groups listen before they answer; and never rank or count prayer.
problem: Prayer apps let people share requests with friends, small groups, a parish or everyone in the app. Requests name illnesses, families and fears, often about people who never agreed to be mentioned. Most are ordinary, and being prayed for is a gift. Some disclose abuse or danger, sometimes involving someone in the same church, and the listener may be a volunteer with a duty to report, a friend who quotes a verse back, or a stranger. Notifications and automatic nudges can carry a request further than the person meant.
solution: Let the person choose the audience before writing, and show who will see the request, for how long and whether it can be edited or deleted. Ask before naming someone else. Offer a route to one chosen person, with what each listener can and must do shown before sending. When a church sets the app up, name its safeguarding contact and keep an independent service beside it. Give groups ways to respond that start with listening, keep support groups’ members confidential, and send no automatic notifications about someone without asking them each time.
failure: A public feed as the default; first names and requests visible to strangers; a request about someone else posted without their consent; friends notified automatically when the app infers a low mood; a leader as the only route for a concern about the leader’s team; verses quoted back at someone who disclosed harm; hearts and counts on requests; streak boards with Praise and Remind buttons; promising confidentiality a listener cannot keep.
test: Ask people to share an ordinary request and something hard, then to name everyone who will see each, for how long, and what each listener must do with it. Read the replies a group gives to a hard request. Find the safeguarding contact and an independent service from inside the app in under a minute. Check what notifications say, and to whom.
faith: Paul asks the church to “rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15), and to “carry one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2). Job’s friends did best when they “sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights, but no one spoke a word to him because they saw how intense his suffering was” (Job 2:13). Hearing a request is a charge as well as a gift. The same passages have been used to press people to share more than they chose, or to keep concerns inside a church, so the listener’s care matters as much as the sharer’s trust.

status: Research-informed design proposal · draft for review
title: Reading together
summary: From the same passage on the same day with nothing shown, through a guide for meeting in person, a group with a leader and a plan with friends, to a feed of friends’ activity and a public thread on the verse: decide what the others see of each person’s reading, and who looks after what is said.
takeaway: Share the passage and the conversation, not the record; say before a plan starts what the others will see, and let people delete it; make falling behind a way back, not a signal; give the conversation a shape that starts with listening; prepare for a verse turned against the person who shared; keep young people’s conversations in the group and name a safeguarding contact; and label strangers’ notes as theirs, a step away from the text.
problem: Bible apps let people read with others: the same passage on the same day, plans with friends that show each day’s ticks, group units led by someone with a code, comments on every verse and feeds of what friends have read. Each decides what the others see of a person’s reading and who looks after the conversation. Ticks make the person who fell behind visible. Comments put strangers’ readings beside the text. A reply can turn a verse against someone who has just shared something hard, and nobody may be there to notice.
solution: Share the passage and the day, and keep each person’s record private unless they choose to show it. Say before a plan starts what participants and friends will see, and let people delete it. Let someone rejoin where the group is today. Give groups prompts that ask what touched each person, not what others should do. When a church or leader runs the group, name who looks after it, keep conversations with young people in the group, and name a safeguarding contact. Label others’ notes as theirs, say who moderates them, and keep them a step away from the text.
failure: Completion ticks for everyone in a group by default; friends’ feeds filled with each completed day that cannot be deleted; no way back for someone who fell behind except by catching up in view of everyone; strangers’ readings shown inside the verse; a verse quoted at someone who shared a hurt, with no one able to step in; leaders messaging young people one to one; badges and streaks in the same stream as the group’s conversation.
test: Run a week of a group plan with five people. Ask each to list what the others can see of them, and where. Have one fall behind and watch what they see when they return. Post a reply that turns a verse against someone who shared, and time how long it takes for someone responsible to notice and reach the person. Check what a young person in the group can receive, and from whom.
faith: Two disciples on the road to Emmaus “talked and deliberated” until Jesus “came up and walked along with them” (Luke 24:15), and afterwards asked each other, “Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32). The first church “devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship” (Acts 2:42). Reading together is a gift, and the conversation needs tending: a verse can open the Scriptures to someone, or be turned against them.

status: Research-informed design proposal · draft for review
title: First use
summary: From opening on a passage, a prayer or a question box with nothing asked, through a first page of places to start, guest use and a short tour, to questions first and payment before the first use: decide what a new person must give, and when, before they reach what they came for.
takeaway: Let people reach what they came for before you ask for anything; ask for an account when there is something to keep, a permission when a feature needs it, and payment after a first use, saying plainly what costs money and why; keep help in a crisis one tap away and never behind an account, a quiz, a quota or a paywall; let “no church right now” be an ordinary answer.
problem: The first minutes in a faith app decide whether someone reads, prays or asks at all. Many apps put a great deal in front of the first verse, prayer or answer: a tour, an account, questions about goals, age and Bible knowledge, testimonials, a request to rate the app, notification and tracking prompts, and a subscription offer. Some people arrive curious; some arrive in a hard night; some come back after years away, or after being hurt in a church. Apps also cost money to build and run, and AI answers cost money every time, so the question of when and how to ask for payment is real, not a trick.
solution: Open on what the person came for: today’s passage, a prayer to play, a question box. Offer a short page of places to start, with help in a crisis at the top. Let people use the app as a guest, and ask for an account when there is something to keep, such as a highlight or a plan. Keep any tour short and skippable. Ask questions only when the answer changes something, and let each be skipped. Ask for permissions when a feature needs them. Ask for payment after a first use: say what is free, what costs money and roughly how much, and give the charge date before a trial begins.
failure: An account, a phone number or a quiz before the first verse; a request to rate the app before it has been used; notification and tracking prompts at launch; a weekly subscription as the default; testimonials and social proof between questions; crisis help behind a sign-up or a quota; questions about church attendance or Bible knowledge that cannot be skipped and that praise every answer; payment framed as the only way to be faithful, or free use framed as the only way to be faithful.
test: Install the app on a fresh phone and count the taps, fields and prompts before the first verse, prayer or answer. Do it again as someone who says, in the first box they see, that they don’t want to be here anymore, and time how long it takes to reach a person. Do it as someone who answers “no church right now”. Write down, for a year of use, what the person pays, what it costs you to serve them, and whether the app says so.
faith: When two disciples began to follow Jesus, he asked them, “What do you want?”, and when they asked where he was staying, he said, “Come and see” (John 1:38–39). They spent the day with him before anything was asked of them. The same Scriptures say both “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matthew 10:8) and “the worker is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7): welcome freely, and pay honestly those who serve.

status: Research-informed design proposal · draft for review
title: Children and families
summary: From a story read aloud with a grown-up, through family time in a general app, a children’s Bible app and games with episodes, to a youth group app with a leader and a child alone with an AI or a public community: decide who is with the child, what the app collects, how it holds attention, and what happens when a child says something worrying.
takeaway: Design for a grown-up beside the child where you can; collect nothing a child does not need to give; keep purchases, links and settings behind a parental gate; switch off streaks, autoplay and notifications for children; tell hard stories with care and room for questions; keep young people’s conversations in a group with two leaders; and when a child writes something worrying, answer the child first, with a helpline and a trusted adult, instead of telling a parent automatically.
problem: Children meet Scripture through apps made for them, family corners of apps made for adults, video and game apps, youth group apps, and adult apps they use anyway, including AI chat apps rated for all ages. Each decides who is with the child, what it collects, how it holds attention and what it does when a child says something worrying. Children’s data is protected by law in the EU, the UK and the US; children’s attention is easy to capture; and a story such as the Flood or the cross can frighten a child who meets it alone. In a youth group, as in any church work with children, contact needs safeguards.
solution: Where you can, design for a grown-up beside the child: a story to read aloud with questions to wonder about together. For a child using the app alone, ask for no account and no personal details, show no ads, keep purchases, links and settings behind a parental gate, and leave out streaks, autoplay and notifications. Tell hard stories with care, and suggest talking them over. For young people in a church group, keep conversations in the group with two leaders, get parents’ consent, and name a safeguarding contact. When a child writes something worrying, answer the child: say it was right to tell, offer a helpline for children and a trusted adult, and, in a church-run app, route it to the trained safeguarding contact, not automatically to a parent.
failure: Accounts, ages and names asked of children; third-party analytics and advertising; purchases and links a child can reach; streaks, badges and autoplay that keep a child watching; frightening scenes labelled “KIDS” with no grown-up in view; one-to-one messages between a leader and a young person; a child left alone with an AI chat or a public comment thread; a worrying message sent automatically to a parent who may be the danger, or answered with nothing.
test: Hand the app to a child of the target age with a grown-up watching, and note every place the child could buy, leave the app, meet a stranger or be asked for a detail. List every piece of data collected and who receives it. Read the Flood or the crucifixion with a five-year-old and see what the app gives the grown-up to say. Type a worrying message as a child would, and walk through who sees it and what the child is told.
faith: When people brought little children to Jesus and the disciples rebuked them, he “was indignant and told them, ‘Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these’” (Mark 10:14). Israel was told to teach God’s words “to your children and speak of them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road” (Deuteronomy 6:7). Jesus also said that whoever causes “one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble” would be better off with “a large millstone hung around his neck” (Matthew 18:6). Children are welcomed, taught at home, and protected.

status: Research-informed design proposal · draft for review
title: Notifications and reminders
summary: From an app that waits to be opened, through reminders the person sets, the church’s hours of prayer, a daily word and messages from people, to notifications tuned to bring people back and an AI that writes first: decide who chooses the interruption, how urgent it claims to be, what it says to someone who has been away, and what reaches someone at night.
takeaway: Let the person decide when they are called: ask for permission when they set a reminder, offer the church’s hours as a shared rhythm, send people’s messages rather than the app’s, and keep quiet hours. Never mark a reminder Time Sensitive, never count down a streak, never write in a persona’s voice to bring someone back, and after silence ask once whether to keep reminding, then stop.
problem: Every faith app that can send notifications has to decide when to interrupt, about what and in whose voice. The phone sits beside the bed, so a notification reaches people at their most unguarded: waking, at work, with their children, awake at night. Notifications are also the strongest tool for bringing people back, and the techniques that work best for that, streak warnings, optimised timing and wording, messages that pretend to miss someone, are the ones that treat prayer as a habit to sell.
solution: Start with the person’s own choice. Ask for permission when someone sets a reminder, not before the first verse, and let them choose the days, the time and the words. Offer the church’s hours, morning, midday and evening, as a rhythm others keep too. Notify for what people did, a prayer said for them, an invitation, not for what the app wants. Mark nothing Time Sensitive that is not, keep quiet hours, and let the phone’s summary and Focus do their work. When someone stops opening the app, ask once whether to keep reminding them, then stop.
failure: A permission prompt before the first verse; “Your 12-day streak ends at midnight!” marked Time Sensitive to break through Sleep Focus; reminders that multiply after silence; “We miss you” and “Did I say something wrong?” in the voice of an app or an AI; reminders to friends who stopped; telling someone’s friends that the app thinks they need a call; marketing offers in the prayer reminder’s place.
test: Install the app on a test phone, allow notifications, use it once and leave it for two weeks. Log every notification: time, words, urgency and who chose it. Then turn on Sleep Focus and a Scheduled Summary and see what breaks through. Finally, read every notification as someone who is grieving, depressed or awake at 2 am would read it.
faith: “Morning, noon, and night, I cry out in distress, and He hears my voice” (Psalm 55:17). Daniel prayed “three times a day” (Daniel 6:10), and the Psalmist “Seven times a day” (Psalm 119:164); the church has rung bells for its hours ever since. But when the disciples found Jesus praying alone and said, “Everyone is looking for You!”, he did not go back (Mark 1:37–38). God spoke to Elijah not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in “a still, small voice” (1 Kings 19:12).

status: Research-informed design proposal · draft for review
title: Giving and offerings
summary: From leaving giving to the church, through a quiet way to give, the church’s offering in the app, a regular gift and showing what a gift does, to a gift tied to an ad-free app and, as the warning case, pressure and promises: decide where the ask appears, what is chosen for the giver, and what the app says a gift will do.
takeaway: Make giving easy to find and never in the way: start with no amount and a one-off gift, say who receives it, what it costs and what it does, send a receipt, and make stopping a regular gift as easy as starting it. Never ask in a crisis, after a prayer request or of a child, never preselect a tip or a tier, and never promise that God will repay a gift.
problem: Giving is worship, and it pays for churches, missions and the apps themselves. More and more of it happens on a phone: through a church’s app, a QR code during the service, or a Give button in a Bible app. The same screens that make generosity easy can also press people: an amount chosen for them, a monthly gift switched on, a tip added on top, a gift tied to an ad-free app, an ask after someone has shared their grief, or the promise that a seed sown now will come back as a harvest.
solution: Put giving where someone looks for it, in a menu or after a service, not in the middle of reading or prayer. Start with an empty amount and a one-off gift; let the person switch on a regular gift and choose its day. Name who receives the gift and what it pays for, show fees as fees, send a receipt, and keep a history the person can stop or change in one place. Speak of what a gift does with current, complete and accurate figures, and say when enough has been given.
failure: A “Most popular” tier ticked in advance; a tip of a sixth of the gift added unless someone slides it to zero; a monthly gift switched on by default; a gift box on the screen after someone shares a prayer request; “Sow a seed of faith today and expect a harvest” beside a countdown; givers ranked by amount; a figure from five years ago presented as today’s; a recurring gift that can only be stopped by email.
test: Give the smallest possible gift in your app as someone new, then as someone who has just lost their job, then as someone who has just shared a prayer request. Write down every amount, tick and toggle that was chosen for you, every place the ask appeared, and how many steps it takes to stop a regular gift. Then read every sentence about what a gift will do, and ask whether you could show the figure’s source and date.
faith: “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Jesus said that the poor widow who put in two small coins “has put more than all the others into the treasury” (Mark 12:43), and told those who give, “do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (Matthew 6:3). When the people brought more than enough for the tabernacle, Moses “sent a proclamation throughout the camp” to stop (Exodus 36:6).

editorial_review.drawback: The tools that raise most, chosen amounts, ticked tiers, added tips, monthly by default, asks at emotional moments and promises of return, press people to give what they did not decide in their heart.

title: AI memory
summary: From an assistant that keeps nothing, through context the person adds and a conversation they can see, to memory they switch on and can see item by item, and a profile the app builds from their prayers as a warning case: decide what the assistant may use, what it keeps, and whether the person can see and change it.
takeaway: Let the person see everything the assistant uses before it answers: the passage, any note or file, the conversation so far and each remembered item. Let memory be switched on once, then show each item in the conversation as it is saved, in its exact words; never keep feelings, health, sins or other people’s stories unless the person asks; let every item be edited and deleted; and never build a profile the person cannot see.
problem: A Bible assistant answers better when it knows what someone is reading, what they asked yesterday and what they are going through. But conversations in faith apps hold confessions, doubts, grief, illness and other people’s private stories. Chat products now remember across conversations, attach files and pages, and infer interests for personalisation. People disclose more to human-like assistants, and their picture of what is kept is often wrong. A remembered sentence can return weeks later in an opening message, a recommendation or an advertisement.
solution: Show context as visible, removable items beside the question: the passage, a note, a file, with what each will be used for. Keep a conversation only where the person can find it and delete it, and say where it is kept. Let people switch memory on or off in one place; when it is on, show each saved item in the conversation with Edit and Delete, and ask separately before keeping anything personal; keep a memory page that lists every item. Exclude special categories by default. Treat text inside attachments as material to read, never as instructions. Do not infer denomination, health, stage of faith or life events, and do not use conversations for marketing.
failure: A plus icon that uploads without saying so; a private journal sent along silently; removed items still used; “Memory updated” with no way to see what; a past loss raised in an opening message; feelings, sins or a friend’s situation remembered without asking; one switch for memory, training and sharing; profiles of “life events” and “faith stage” built from chats; recommendations and offers drawn from what someone confided; text in an attachment obeyed as an instruction.
test: Ask a personal question, then ask the person what the assistant now knows about them and where it is kept; compare with storage, logs and derived data. Remove an attachment and check it was not used. Decline a memory, edit one, delete one, then return the next day. Put an instruction inside an attached file and check it is not followed. Ask a pastor to read the memory page aloud and say whether it is something a friend would keep.
faith: “O LORD, You have searched me and known me” (Psalm 139:1): to be fully known is what God alone does, and does in love. Among people, trust is kept by discretion: “a gossip reveals a secret, but a trustworthy person keeps a confidence” (Proverbs 11:13), and the church has guarded confession with a seal it calls inviolable. God also promises to forget: “I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more” (Hebrews 8:12). An assistant should know only what it is given for the task, keep only what the person chooses, and be able to forget.

editorial_review.purpose: Someone asks an assistant about a passage or their life, and the assistant uses context, a conversation or remembered details to answer.
editorial_review.benefit: Context makes answers specific; continuity saves repeating oneself; a remembered reading plan or question can make the next conversation easier.
editorial_review.drawback: Faith conversations hold confessions, health, doubt and other people’s stories; invisible memory and inferred profiles turn them into data that can resurface, leak or be sold.
editorial_review.differences: A student preparing a talk, someone praying in grief, a teenager, a person in an abusive home and someone sharing a phone need very different defaults.

title: Adjust reading settings without losing the passage
summary: Keep typography, appearance and text-layer preferences close to the reading experience.
takeaway: Let people judge changes against the passage they are reading, and preserve their place when the text reflows.
problem: Leaving the reader to change typography separates the choice from its effect. A crowded settings drawer can obscure the text, while a font-size change can move the reader to an unrelated line.
solution: Offer a labelled reading-settings entry near the passage. A bottom drawer keeps some context visible on mobile; a side panel can retain more readable context on wider screens. Preview typography and appearance against real text. Group font, size and spacing separately from optional verse numbers, notes and section headings. Preserve the semantic reading anchor after reflow. Explain whether changes apply immediately, provide reset, and distinguish persistent preferences from a temporary view.
failure: Tiny slider-only adjustments; unlabeled spacing icons; hiding verse numbers and losing reference access; hiding a note marker as though the note were deleted; fixed drawer height that clips controls at large text; changing edition while claiming to change appearance.
test: Open settings midway through a long chapter, increase text size, change spacing and hide verse numbers. Dismiss and locate the same verse. Repeat with keyboard, screen reader, narrow viewport, poetry and large system text. Test reset and returning after restart if persistence is promised.
faith: A quiet layout is a preference, not a measure of spiritual seriousness. Notes, red-letter styling and editorial headings influence interpretation; let people understand which layers they are changing without implying that hiding them removes Scripture.
flow: Open reading settings from the current passage.
Adjust a clearly labelled preference and inspect the effect.
Keep the same reference visible when typography reflows.
Dismiss or reset, then continue reading; preserve preferences only as explained.
